html:
Can frontier models do exact quantum-tunnelling physics without a computer?

Domain: nanoelectronics · 13 closed-book tasks · graded by code against exact references

4 Claude models, 2 effort levels, 1 open model · honest result: I did not find the gap
say: Can frontier language models do exact quantum tunnelling physics without a computer? I am a physics undergraduate, and this is my entry for the micro1 Eval Hackathon. I built thirteen closed book tasks in nanoelectronics, graded every answer by code against exact references, and tested four Claude models plus a small open model. Spoiler: I set out to find a limitation, and for the frontier models I did not find one. This video shows what I built, why you can trust the numbers, and what I did learn.

html:
Why it matters

  • Tunnel oxides, resonant tunnelling diodes, STM, molecular junctions
  • A 0.3 eV error in a barrier changes the current by a factor of 2
  • One decade of current per 0.2 nm of oxide
  • Engineers use a transfer-matrix code. Can a model be trusted as a first-pass calculator?
say: Why does this matter? In tunnel oxides, resonant tunnelling diodes, scanning tunnelling microscopes and molecular junctions, small errors in the physics become big errors in the current. A three tenths of an electron volt error in a barrier height changes a tunnelling current by about a factor of two, and every two tenths of a nanometre of oxide costs about a decade of current. Engineers normally use a transfer matrix program. The question is whether a model can be trusted as a quick first pass calculator, giving the exact number, not an approximation.

html:
A task and its grader

GaAs / AlGaAs / GaAs: m* = 0.067 m0 in the contacts,
0.092 m0 in the barrier, V0 = 0.30 eV, a = 3.0 nm,
E = 0.10 eV. Use the matching conditions appropriate
for position-dependent mass. Exact T?

reference 0.05801  |  psi' continuous (wrong): 0.04755
  • Last line ANSWER: {"T": ...}, 3% tolerance, outcome only
  • Wrong-method detectors label every failure
  • 66 grader tests · 2 independent solvers check every reference
say: Here is one task. An electron crosses an aluminium gallium arsenide barrier between gallium arsenide contacts, with different effective masses, and the model must use the right boundary conditions and report the exact transmission. The reference is zero point zero five eight zero one. The naive boundary condition gives zero point zero four seven five five, eighteen percent off, so it fails. The grader reads only the last answer line, compares it with a three percent tolerance, and grades the outcome, not the method. If an answer misses, it is compared with what common wrong methods give, so every failure is labelled. Sixty six unit tests check the grader, including deliberately wrong answers. And every reference is recomputed with a second solver, using explicit wave amplitudes and an analytic resonance condition.

Results: default reasoning effort

modeltrials correct
Haiku 5.538 / 39
Sonnet 5.539 / 39
Opus 5.539 / 39
Fable 5.139 / 39
qwen2.5 3B (open, CPU)2 / 39

13 tasks · 3 trials each · no tools · low effort: 37, 39, 38, 38 of 39
say: The results. At default reasoning effort, Sonnet, Opus and Fable got all thirty nine trials right. Haiku missed one. The small three billion parameter open model got two out of thirty nine. At low reasoning effort the Claude models scored thirty seven, thirty nine, thirty eight and thirty eight out of thirty nine. So there is a clear spread between a small model and the frontier models, but almost no headroom among the frontier models. I tested tools off, thirteen tasks, three trials each, and I do not claim a ranking among the Claude models.

html:
Failure analysis

  • Haiku, oxide task: effective mass in the denominator of the decay constant, kappa 13.9 instead of 5.85
  • At low effort, 3 of 4 misses: an exact calculation replaced by a named approximation, flagged in a caveat, number still given as the answer
  • Opus: Lorentzian width, 0.0142 vs 0.0164 eV
  • Haiku: Herring formula, 69 vs 54.5 meV
  • 3B model: format failures, T = 1 for an asymmetric structure, wrong numbers
say: What did the failures look like? Haiku once put the effective mass in the denominator of the decay constant, so a heavier electron tunnelled more, which is the wrong direction. At low reasoning effort there were four misses, and in three of them the model replaced the exact calculation I asked for by a named approximation. Opus used a Lorentzian estimate for the resonance width. Haiku used the Herring formula for the splitting. Each one said in a caveat that this was only an estimate, and each one still put a single number on the answer line. The small open model fails differently: it breaks the answer format, assumes full transmission on resonance for an asymmetric structure, or just writes wrong numbers.

html:
I was wrong first

  • First run: 0 of 12 trials passed the resonance task
  • 11 of 12 trials gave 0.0862 eV. My reference said 0.0818 eV
  • Cause: my helper gave the contacts the free-electron mass
  • Independent analytic resonance condition: the models were right
  • Fixed, re-graded without new model calls, first-pass grades kept
say: There is one more finding, and it is about me. In my first run, all four models failed the resonance energy task, in twelve out of twelve trials. Eleven of those trials gave the same answer, zero point zero eight six two electron volts, and my reference said zero point zero eight one eight. The guide says a zero percent pass rate everywhere is a warning sign, so I checked my reference with an independent analytic resonance condition. The models were right and I was wrong: my helper function had given the contacts the free electron mass. I fixed it, re-graded the stored outputs without any new model calls, and kept the first pass grades in the files.

html:
Takeaway

  • Closed-book textbook quantum mechanics is no longer where frontier models fail
  • Remaining risk: commitment to exactness. A bare number is not an exact number
  • Graders that read only the number cannot see the caveat. Score “declared approximation” separately
  • In this domain a bug in the reference is now likelier than a model error. Use a second solver
say: My takeaway. Closed book, textbook level quantum mechanics is no longer where these frontier models fail. One Haiku trial used about thirty seven thousand hidden reasoning tokens to sum Airy function series by hand and still got the answer right. The remaining risk is commitment to exactness: when pushed, a model may swap in an approximation, mention it in a caveat, and still hand you one number. A grader that only reads the number cannot see that, so eval authors should score declared approximations separately. And a bug in the reference is now more likely than a mistake by the model, so build a second solver.

html:
Reproduce it

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pytest -q graders
python reference/independent_check.py
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... python run_eval.py \
   --backend anthropic --models claude-sonnet-5-5

Raw outputs and transcripts of every trial are in the ZIP. The API backend was not run against a live API; the results used the Claude Code CLI backend. AI use: Claude drafted everything, I have not yet reviewed every task, and the README says so.
say: To reproduce it, install the requirements, run the grader tests, run the independent check of the references, and run the harness with your own API key. Raw outputs and transcripts of every trial are in the zip. Two honest notes. First, the API backends of my harness were not tested against a live API, the results come from the Claude Code command line backend. Second, Claude drafted the tasks, the code and this write up on my instruction, and I have not yet reviewed every task myself. The README says so, and explains how I checked the work instead. Thank you for watching.
